author: KERNAL Content Team
title: Cross-Validation
subtitle: K-fold, stratified folds, and avoiding data leakage

whyItExists.problem: A single train/test split is unreliable — it depends on which samples ended up in each set by chance. You could get lucky or unlucky and completely misjudge how good your model really is.
whyItExists.solution: Cross-validation evaluates the model on multiple different train/test splits and averages the results. This gives a much more reliable performance estimate and also uses all data for both training and validation.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Whenever comparing models, selecting hyperparameters, or reporting model performance — especially on small to medium datasets where a single split is too noisy.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: When the dataset is very large (millions of rows) and a single hold-out test set is statistically stable. CV is computationally expensive on large datasets.

explainModes.beginner: Instead of splitting your data once, cross-validation splits it 5 times, each time using a different chunk as the test set. The 5 scores are averaged. This is like taking an exam 5 times with different questions and averaging your grade for a fairer assessment.
explainModes.simple: K-fold CV divides data into K equal parts (folds). It trains K times: each time using K-1 folds for training and 1 fold for testing. The results are averaged. This reduces the luck factor of a single split.
explainModes.standard: K-fold CV provides an unbiased estimate of test error by rotating through K train/test splits. Stratified K-fold preserves class ratios. Pipeline integration prevents preprocessing leakage across folds.
explainModes.technical: CV minimises both optimistic bias (from a lucky split) and pessimistic bias (from a small training set). Nested CV separates hyperparameter selection (inner loop) from model assessment (outer loop) to avoid selection bias.
explainModes.deepDive: K-fold CV is a nearly unbiased estimator of the generalisation error but has high variance for small K. Leave-One-Out CV is unbiased but computationally expensive and has high variance. Repeated K-fold averages multiple independent K-fold runs, trading cost for stability.

content.text: A single train/test split is unreliable. If your test set happens to contain easy examples, you overestimate performance. If it contains hard ones, you underestimate. Cross-validation evaluates the model on multiple independent splits and averages the results for a fairer estimate.

content.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
import numpy as np

model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=42)

# Simple 5-fold (not stratified)
kf = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=kf, scoring='f1')
print(f'F1 (5-fold):   {scores.mean():.3f} ± {scores.std():.3f}')

# Stratified — preserves class ratios in each fold (use for classification)
skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
st_scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=skf, scoring='f1')
print(f'F1 (stratified): {st_scores.mean():.3f} ± {st_scores.std():.3f}')

content.text: If you scale the data before cross-validation, the scaler sees the test fold's statistics — this is data leakage. Using a Pipeline ensures that preprocessing is re-fit inside each fold on the training data only.

from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold

# Pipeline: scaler is fit inside each CV fold, preventing leakage
pipe = Pipeline([
    ('scaler', StandardScaler()),
    ('model', LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
])

skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=skf, scoring='roc_auc')
print(f'AUC-ROC: {scores.mean():.3f} ± {scores.std():.3f}')

from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

pipe = Pipeline([
    ('scaler', StandardScaler()),
    ('rf', RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42))
])

param_grid = {
    'rf__n_estimators': [50, 100, 200],
    'rf__max_depth': [5, 10, None],
    'rf__min_samples_leaf': [1, 5, 10]
}

search = GridSearchCV(
    pipe,
    param_grid,
    cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42),
    scoring='f1',
    n_jobs=-1,     # use all CPU cores
    verbose=1
)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f'Best params: {search.best_params_}')
print(f'Best CV F1:  {search.best_score_:.3f}')

from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
from scipy.stats import randint, uniform

# When the grid is too large for exhaustive search
param_dist = {
    'rf__n_estimators': randint(50, 500),
    'rf__max_depth': [5, 10, 20, None],
    'rf__min_samples_leaf': randint(1, 20),
    'rf__max_features': uniform(0.3, 0.7)  # fraction of features
}

rand_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    pipe,
    param_dist,
    n_iter=50,     # sample 50 random combinations
    cv=5,
    scoring='f1',
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)
rand_search.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(f'Best CV F1: {rand_search.best_score_:.3f}')

content.text: Always use a Pipeline when cross-validating. Any step that fits from data (scaler, imputer, encoder) must be inside the pipeline so it only sees training folds, not the test fold.

Don't use the test set for hyperparameter selection. Use cross-validation on the training set to pick hyperparameters, then evaluate on the test set exactly once at the end. Using the test set for tuning inflates your performance estimate.

questions.question: What does 5-fold cross-validation do?
options: Trains 5 separate models on all data and picks the best
Splits data into 5 folds and trains/tests 5 times, averaging results
Splits data into 5 random sets and picks the best
questions.explanation: 5-fold CV splits data into 5 equal parts. Each fold serves once as the test set while the other 4 train the model. The 5 scores are averaged for a stable estimate.

questions.question: Why should preprocessing be inside a Pipeline during cross-validation?
options: To prevent the scaler from seeing test-fold statistics during fitting
Because sklearn requires it for CV
questions.explanation: If you scale before CV, the scaler's mean and std are computed from the full dataset including test folds. A Pipeline refits the scaler inside each fold on training data only.

questions.question: When should you use StratifiedKFold over KFold?
options: When you have more than 1000 samples
For classification tasks to ensure each fold has the same class proportions
questions.explanation: StratifiedKFold ensures each fold contains approximately the same proportion of each class as the full dataset. This is especially important for imbalanced classification problems.

faq.q: What is a Pipeline in scikit-learn?
faq.a: A Pipeline chains preprocessing steps and the model together so they can be fitted and cross-validated as a single unit. This prevents data leakage by ensuring preprocessing is only fitted on training folds.

faq.q: How many folds should I use?
faq.a: 5 or 10 folds are the standard. More folds give a lower-bias estimate but take longer. Use 10 for small datasets where you need more training data per fold. For very large datasets, 5 or even 3 folds may be sufficient.

faq.q: What is the difference between GridSearchCV and RandomizedSearchCV?
faq.a: GridSearchCV tries every combination of hyperparameters exhaustively — good when the grid is small. RandomizedSearchCV samples a fixed number of random combinations — faster for large grids, and often finds near-optimal settings with fewer trials.
